## Introduction

Predicting whether a customer will churn is a common classification task, but it
throws away a crucial dimension: *when*. Two customers flagged as "will churn" are
not equivalent if one is likely to leave next month and the other in two years —
yet a standard classifier treats them the same. Survival analysis keeps the time
dimension intact, modeling not just whether a customer churns but how long they
are expected to stay, and which factors accelerate or delay that outcome.

This project analyzes churn in a telecom customer base (n = 7,032) using three
methods of increasing flexibility: Kaplan-Meier curves for a model-free view of
survival, Cox Proportional Hazards for an interpretable parametric model, and
Random Survival Forest to test whether relaxing Cox's linearity assumption
improves predictive performance. The guiding question is not just "what predicts
churn," but "does a more flexible, less interpretable model actually earn its
complexity here."

## Data

<!--
- Dataset: Telco Customer Churn (Kaggle) or your own.
- Required columns: tenure (duration), Churn (event indicator), covariates.
- Note censoring: customers still active at data collection = censored, not "no event".
-->

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(survival)
library(survminer)
library(randomForestSRC)
library(ggRandomForests)

df <- read_csv("data/WA_Fn-UseC_-Telco-Customer-Churn.csv")  # update path
glimpse(df)
```

```{r}
# Basic cleaning
# - TotalCharges is stored as character with 11 blank (" ") entries, all at
#   tenure = 0 (brand-new customers, never billed). These have no observed
#   survival time, so they're dropped rather than imputed.
# - Churn recoded to 0/1 event indicator.
# - customerID kept for reference but excluded from modeling formulas.
# - SeniorCitizen cast to factor (stored as 0/1 int, but categorical).

df <- df %>%
  filter(tenure > 0) %>%
  mutate(
    Churn = ifelse(Churn == "Yes", 1, 0),
    TotalCharges = as.numeric(TotalCharges),
    SeniorCitizen = factor(SeniorCitizen, labels = c("No", "Yes"))
  )

summary(df)
```

### Censoring check

<!-- Show proportion censored vs event observed -- standard in a survival
     write-up, reviewers will look for it. -->

```{r}
event_rate <- mean(df$Churn)
cat(sprintf("Event (churn) rate: %.2f%%\n", event_rate * 100))
cat(sprintf("Censored rate: %.2f%%\n", (1 - event_rate) * 100))
```

Roughly 27% of customers in this sample have churned (observed events); the
remaining 73% are censored — still active as of data collection, meaning their
true tenure is at least as long as recorded but not yet fully known. This is a
normal and expected censoring rate for subscription-churn data and confirms the
dataset is a legitimate fit for survival methods rather than plain classification.

## Exploratory Analysis

```{r}
ggplot(df, aes(x = tenure, fill = factor(Churn))) +
  geom_histogram(alpha = 0.6, position = "identity", bins = 30) +
  labs(x = "Tenure (months)", y = "Count", fill = "Churned") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Kaplan-Meier Estimation

<!--
- Overall survival curve.
- Segmented KM curves by a key categorical variable (e.g. Contract type).
- Log-rank test to confirm segments differ significantly.
-->

```{r}
km_fit <- survfit(Surv(tenure, Churn) ~ 1, data = df)

ggsurvplot(
  km_fit,
  data = df,
  title = "Overall Survival Curve",
  xlab = "Tenure (months)",
  ylab = "Survival Probability"
)
```

```{r}
# Segmented by a key variable -- update column name if needed
km_fit_group <- survfit(Surv(tenure, Churn) ~ Contract, data = df)

ggsurvplot(
  km_fit_group,
  data = df,
  pval = TRUE,
  risk.table = TRUE,
  title = "Survival Curves by Contract Type"
)
```

The segmented curves show a clear, substantial separation by contract type: 
month-to-month customers churn far faster than one- or two-year contract holders,
with the log-rank test confirming this difference is statistically significant.
This is the single clearest signal in the dataset and foreshadows the Cox model's
largest hazard ratios below — contract length is doing most of the predictive
work on its own.

## Cox Proportional Hazards Model

```{r}
# customerID excluded -- identifier, not a predictor.
# TotalCharges excluded -- it is approximately tenure x MonthlyCharges, so it
# directly encodes the survival duration itself; including it as a predictor
# leaks the outcome and inflates concordance artificially.
# "No internet service" / "No phone service" levels collapsed to "No" --
# these are perfectly redundant with InternetService == "No" / PhoneService
# == "No" already in the model, which produced NA coefficients (collinearity).
# Character columns converted to factor -- required by randomForestSRC, and
# cleaner for coxph too (avoids implicit string handling).
df_model <- df %>%
  select(-customerID, -TotalCharges) %>%
  mutate(
    across(
      c(MultipleLines, OnlineSecurity, OnlineBackup, DeviceProtection,
        TechSupport, StreamingTV, StreamingMovies),
      ~ recode(.x, "No internet service" = "No", "No phone service" = "No")
    ),
    across(where(is.character), as.factor)
  )

cox_fit <- coxph(Surv(tenure, Churn) ~ ., data = df_model)
summary(cox_fit)
```

The strongest effects on churn hazard:

- **Contract length dominates.** Relative to month-to-month, one-year contracts
  cut churn hazard by ~80% (HR = 0.20), and two-year contracts by ~96%
  (HR = 0.04). This is by far the largest effect in the model.
- **Payment method matters.** Customers paying by electronic check or mailed
  check have roughly 1.8x the churn hazard of those on automatic bank transfer,
  suggesting payment friction (or the customer segment that chooses manual
  payment) is a meaningful retention signal.
- **Add-on services reduce hazard.** Having online security (HR = 0.54), online
  backup (HR = 0.54), or tech support (HR = 0.69) is each associated with
  roughly 30-45% lower churn hazard — customers more embedded in the service
  ecosystem churn less.
- **Having a partner reduces hazard** (HR = 0.60) — a demographic/stability
  signal independent of service usage.
- Internet service type and streaming add-ons (TV, Movies) were not
  statistically significant once other covariates were accounted for.

Model concordance is 0.866 — strong discriminative ability for a churn model,
without relying on any variable that leaks the outcome's time axis.


### Proportional Hazards Assumption Check

<!--
This is the step most portfolio projects skip. Including it signals rigor.
-->

```{r}
ph_test <- cox.zph(cox_fit)
ph_test
ggcoxzph(ph_test)
```

With n = 7,032, the cox.zph global test is statistically significant
(p < 2e-16), and most individual covariates show significant chi-squared
values. This is expected and should not be read as "the PH assumption fails" --
with a sample this large, even trivially small time-varying deviations register
as significant. A handful of covariates (gender, SeniorCitizen, Dependents,
Contract) show no significant deviation, meaning their effect on hazard is
stable over the follow-up period. For the covariates with large chi-squared
values (MonthlyCharges, the internet/online-service bundle), the practical
question is whether the ggcoxzph plots show a meaningful trend over time or
just a mild one — not visible from the test alone, but based on the magnitude
of the chi-squared statistics, these are the variables most worth stratifying
on if this model were deployed in production rather than used for a portfolio
demonstration.

## Random Survival Forest (Flexible Alternative)

<!--
Motivation: Cox assumes a linear, additive log-hazard. RSF relaxes this,
capturing nonlinear effects and interactions without specifying a functional
form -- same "classical vs. flexible model" theme as the GARCH-RNN project.
-->

```{r}
rsf_fit <- rfsrc(
  Surv(tenure, Churn) ~ .,
  data = df_model,
  ntree = 500,
  importance = TRUE
)

print(rsf_fit)
```

The RSF achieves an out-of-bag concordance of 0.842, compared to 0.866 for the
Cox model above -- Cox outperforms the more flexible RSF on this dataset. This
is a legitimate and informative result, not a failure of the RSF: it suggests
the relationships driving churn here (contract length, payment method, add-on
services) are close enough to linear and additive that Cox's simpler, fully
interpretable model captures them as well as or better than a model built to
find nonlinear interactions. The added flexibility of RSF does not pay for
itself on this dataset.

### Variable Importance

```{r}
plot(gg_vimp(rsf_fit))
```

## Model Comparison

<!--
Primary metric: concordance index (C-index) -- standard in survival analysis,
NOT accuracy/AUC. Compare Cox PH vs RSF on held-out test set (or OOB for RSF).
-->

```{r}
# Cox concordance (from model summary, or recompute on held-out test set)
cox_c_index <- summary(cox_fit)$concordance["C"]

# RSF out-of-bag concordance
rsf_c_index <- 1 - rsf_fit$err.rate[length(rsf_fit$err.rate)]

cat(sprintf("Cox PH C-index: %.4f\n", cox_c_index))
cat(sprintf("RSF C-index: %.4f\n", rsf_c_index))
```

|  Model | C-index |
|--------|---------|
| Cox PH | 0.8664  |
| RSF    | 0.8415  |

Cox PH wins by a small but consistent margin. Combined with the PH-assumption
check above, this points to the same conclusion as the GARCH-RNN project's
flat-likelihood finding: added model flexibility is not automatically better --
it earns its place only when the underlying relationships genuinely require it.
Here, they largely don't.

## Business Takeaway

The highest-risk segment is clear from the Cox model: month-to-month customers
paying by electronic or mailed check, without online security or tech support
add-ons. Relative to a customer with a two-year contract, automatic payment,
and both add-ons, this profile carries a churn hazard many times higher once
the individual hazard ratios are compounded.

Two concrete actions follow directly from the model:

1. **Target contract conversion first.** Since contract length produces by far
   the largest hazard reduction, incentivizing month-to-month customers to move
   to even a one-year contract (not necessarily two-year) captures most of the
   available retention benefit.
2. **Bundle add-on services into retention offers.** Online security and tech
   support are each associated with ~30-45% lower hazard independent of
   contract type -- offering these as a retention incentive (rather than a
   discount alone) targets a mechanism the data shows actually works, not just
   a price lever.

Payment method is also actionable: nudging electronic/mailed-check customers
toward automatic payment could plausibly reduce churn, though this should be
treated as a correlational signal, not a proven causal lever, without a
controlled test.

## Conclusion

This analysis modeled telecom customer churn as a time-to-event process rather
than a binary outcome, using Kaplan-Meier curves, Cox Proportional Hazards, and
Random Survival Forest. Contract length and service add-ons emerged as the
strongest retention levers, and -- after removing a leakage-prone variable
(TotalCharges) and resolving a collinearity issue in the service-bundle
features -- the Cox model reached a concordance of 0.866, slightly outperforming
the more flexible RSF (0.842). The practical implication is twofold: the
underlying churn relationships in this dataset are close to linear, making Cox
both the more interpretable and the better-performing choice here, and the
clearest retention lever available to the business is contract-length
conversion, not individual pricing adjustments.
